units.title: Range and hash partitioning
outcomes: Choose range, hash or compound-key partitioning for a stated access pattern from scan fan-out and write spread.
Explain when a compound key keeps a range scan on one shard under hash partitioning.
State the fixed-shard-count trade-off between cheap moves, split cost and the growth limit.
units.why: Partitioning decides which machine answers each key. The Systems unit on partitioning, hot keys, rebalancing and stale writers taught range and hash placement, modulo movement and fixed shards. Here the new work is choosing a scheme from two contrasting access patterns and writing the decision down, including compound keys and the growth limit of a fixed shard count.

next.note: Replace mod-N with a ring when nodes join and leave.
Look shards up in a versioned map instead of recomputing placement.

study.title: Sharding by key range and by hash of key
study.locator: Chapter 7, Sharding of Key-Value Data (pp. 255-262): Sharding by Key Range, Rebalancing key-range sharded data, Sharding by Hash of Key with Figures 7-2 and 7-3, plus Fixed number of shards and Sharding by hash range
study.depth: Skim the range and modulo pages you read for the Systems unit; read Sharding by hash range and its compound-key paragraph closely. Stop before Consistent hashing (p. 263); the next unit derives it.

study.title: Sharding strategies and choosing a partition key
study.locator: Sharding strategies (range, hash, consistent-hash, directory, geographic) and Choosing partition key: high-cardinality, stable keys that appear in queries

study.title: Why one database stops being enough
study.locator: The opening: vertical scaling limits, read replicas, and why data is divided across servers
study.depth: Use as vocabulary for the sharding decision. The routing math comes from DDIA and the drill below.

focus: Range partitioning keeps contiguous keys together, so a scan visits only the shards whose ranges overlap it. Sequential keys such as timestamps can concentrate writes on the newest shard.

Hashing the partition key spreads writes but loses its order, so a range over that key visits every shard. A compound key keeps a range over its later columns on one shard when the query fixes the partition key (DDIA p. 261).
Mod-N placement couples every key to the node count: adding one node reassigns most keys, as Figure 7-3 shows.
Fixed shard counts decouple keys from nodes so only whole shards move, but no cluster can use more nodes than shards, and a wrong initial count forces expensive resharding.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a decision table for two access patterns: sensor readings written every second and read as one sensor's last hour, and user profiles read and written by user ID. For range by timestamp, hash of the whole key and a compound key (hash of the sensor ID, then timestamp), give the shards one write touches, the shards one sensor's hour scan touches, and what a split costs. Then route keys 1 to 8 with `key % 3` to get loads `[2, 3, 3]`.
traps: Hashing the key does not remove skew. It removes correlation between key order and placement; a hot key stays hot on whichever shard owns it.
More shards are not free. Each shard adds metadata and recovery work; DDIA warns the size must be just right, neither too big nor too small.
Assuming every range query fans out under hashing. Only a range over the hashed key does; a compound key keeps a range over later columns on one shard when the query fixes the partition key.

selfTest.q: Sensor writes keyed by timestamp land on one shard under range partitioning. Why, and what key change spreads them?
selfTest.a: Time-contiguous keys fall in one range, so the current shard takes all writes. Prefix each timestamp with the sensor ID so ordering is by sensor then time; each sensor then needs its own range scan afterward.

selfTest.q: Keys 1 to 8 route by `key % 3`. What are the shard loads?
selfTest.a: Shard 0 holds 3 and 6, shard 1 holds 1, 4 and 7, shard 2 holds 2, 5 and 8, so `[2, 3, 3]`.

selfTest.q: A 10-node cluster holds 1,000 fixed shards and adds an 11th node. What moves?
selfTest.a: Only whole shards move from old nodes to the new one until shares even out. No key changes shard; only the shard-to-node assignment changes.

selfTest.q: Why can a cluster hold fewer nodes than shards but never usefully more?
selfTest.a: Each node serves whole shards, so a node with no shard serves nothing. Splitting shards to make room is the expensive reshard operation.

practice.name: AlgoMaster Calculate Hash Shard Load
practice.locator: Implement `shardLoads(keys, numShards)` routing each key to `key % numShards`. Example 1 ([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], 3) gives `[2, 3, 3]`; Example 2 ([10, 20, 30, 40], 4) gives `[2, 0, 2, 0]`
practice.note: This drills mod-N routing only. Rings, movement and skew arrive in later units.

units.stopWhen: You fill the decision table for both access patterns without notes and can state the growth limit of your fixed shard count.

fit.note: The Systems partitioning unit is the prerequisite; DDIA's hash-range and compound-key pages with the HLD key criteria support the decision table, and the drill checks routing.

units.title: Consistent hashing rings, rendezvous hashing and weighted virtual nodes
outcomes: Derive key movement for a node join and leave under mod-N, ring and rendezvous placement.
Implement a hash ring with virtual nodes that maps each key to its clockwise owner.
Size virtual-node counts and weights so uneven machines take proportional shares.
units.why: Mod-N placement reshuffles nearly every key on each membership change. Rings and rendezvous move only the keys the new owner takes over, which is what makes adding capacity affordable.

next.note: Run the ring behind a versioned map with redirects.
Move the ranges the ring reassigns under epoch fencing.

study.title: The consistent hashing contract in two paragraphs
study.locator: Chapter 7, Consistent hashing (p. 263): the two properties (roughly equal keys per shard, minimal movement on change) and the pointers to rendezvous and jump hashing
study.depth: Read for the definition only. The derivations come from the HLD chapter; DDIA names rendezvous hashing without deriving it.

study.title: Rings, virtual nodes, bounded load and rendezvous
study.locator: Why modulo hashing breaks, The hash ring (successor lookup and its join-movement estimate), Virtual nodes (\(V \ge 100\) guidance, the simulation figure of about 10 percent standard deviation at \(V = 100\), heterogeneous weights as more entries), Rendezvous/HRW (one score per node, minimal disruption) and the Trade-offs table
study.depth: The chapter's \(1/N\) join estimate is loose: with \(N\) equal nodes before the join, the new node takes an expected \(1/(N+1)\) of keys. The 10 percent figure is a reported simulation, not a bound.

study.title: The five-server cache problem
study.locator: The problem: five cache servers, one key to one server, and why membership changes must move few profiles
study.depth: Use for intuition. The movement math comes from the HLD chapter.

focus: A ring maps keys and nodes to one circle and each key belongs to the first node clockwise. A join at one ring position steals one arc from its successor, and a node with virtual nodes steals one arc per position; a leave hands each arc to its successor.
Virtual nodes give each physical node many scattered ring positions. Weight is just more positions per strong machine, for example twice the entries for a weight-2 host.
Rendezvous scores every node per key and takes the maximum: no ring state, but lookup costs one hash per node, so it fits small clusters.
Consistent here means key stability, not replica or ACID consistency. Rings balance keys, not requests; a hot key still lands on one owner.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, show keys 0 to 7 moving 5 records when shards go from 3 to 4 under mod-N, then show why a ring join moves only the stolen arcs (an expected \(1/(N+1)\) of keys when \(N\) equal nodes become \(N + 1\)). Price lookups as ring binary search in \(O(\log(V \cdot N))\) against rendezvous at \(O(N)\) hashes.
traps: Treating consistent hashing as a hot-key fix. It bounds movement on membership change; a popular key still lands on one owner.
Running one ring position per node. With `V = 1` one node can take 3 times its fair share; the chapter suggests `V >= 100` for caches.
Letting two deciders use different member lists under rendezvous. The same key then maps to different owners, which is a membership problem for the next unit.

selfTest.q: Keys 0 to 7 move from 3 to 4 shards under mod-N. How many move, and what would a ring move instead?
selfTest.a: Five move under mod-N; only 0, 1 and 2 stay. A ring join moves only the keys in the stolen arc, about one new share, and every other key stays put.

selfTest.q: Two physical nodes of equal capacity own 70 and 30 percent of a ring. What is the fix, what does it cost, and when do weights apply instead?
selfTest.a: Give each node many scattered virtual nodes and measure the new shares; the chapter's cited simulations report about 10 percent standard deviation at 100 per node, not a bound. The cost is ring memory, one entry per virtual node. Weights, meaning vnode counts in proportion to capacity, are for unequal machines, not for this imbalance.

selfTest.q: Rendezvous over 5 nodes versus 5,000: what changes per lookup?
selfTest.a: Five score computations against 5,000. Lookup is linear in node count, so rendezvous fits the small cluster and the ring fits the large one.

selfTest.q: Two clients hold different member lists under rendezvous. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The same key maps to different owners, so reads miss and writes split. Both deciders need one current list, which the partition map supplies.

practice.name: Building Distributed Systems: consistent hashing for sharding (RA-2)
practice.locator: Place shards on a hash ring, hash each key to a ring position, and take the next shard clockwise
practice.note: Free browser-graded drill. Keep your own ring with virtual nodes and seeded keys as the evidence.

practice.name: AlgoMaster Count Keys Moved by Resharding
practice.locator: Implement `keysMoved(keys, oldShards, newShards)`. Example 1 ([0 to 7], 3, 4) gives 5; Example 2 ([10, 20, 30, 40], 4, 5) gives 2
practice.note: Counts mod-N movement only. Contrast each result with what your ring moves for the same join.

units.stopWhen: Your ring routes a seeded key set, a join moves only the new range, and you can price mod-N against ring and rendezvous on movement and lookup.

fit.note: DDIA states the contract; the HLD chapter derives ring, virtual-node and rendezvous math, and the two drills check placement and movement.

units.title: Versioned partition maps, routing and redirects under stale configuration, with movement tests
outcomes: Implement a versioned partition map with atomic installation and per-key routing.
Recover stale clients through redirects and map refresh instead of failed writes.
Test single ownership and no lost keys across a move, including stale routes and delayed operations.
units.why: Hashes name shards; maps own them. A versioned map lets ownership move while requests are in flight, and turns stale caches into retried redirects instead of lost writes.

next.note: Rebalance shards under epoch fencing.
Carry map versions into partition ownership and visibility.

study.title: Request routing and who tracks assignments
study.locator: Chapter 7, Request Routing (pp. 265-267): the three routing approaches, who decides placement, the cutover problem, and Figure 7-8 on ZooKeeper-tracked assignment with the gossip alternative

study.title: Numbered configs with redirect and retry
study.locator: Lab 5 Sharded KV (Spring 2026): the ShardConfig number ordering, the shardkv clerk with Query plus ErrWrongGroup retry, and ChangeConfigTo as FreezeShard, InstallShard and DeleteShard fenced by number

study.title: Partition routing and rebalance contract
study.locator: Milestone C: partition routing with reassignment without lost ownership; the stretch goal adds partition rebalance with ownership epochs

focus: Every routing decision reads a numbered map version. In Lab 5 a wrong-owner reply carries no number, so the clerk re-queries the controller; your own fixture may also stamp replies with the installed version.
Wrong-owner contact is a redirect, not an error. The client fetches the new config and retries, as the shardkv clerk does on `ErrWrongGroup`.

Config numbers order assignments but do not revoke an old owner by themselves. Freeze the source before the destination accepts writes, persist that fence with the shard state, and reject stale migration RPCs.
Gossip-disseminated maps can split brain with two owners for one shard. Consensus-tracked maps cost more but give one authoritative version.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the routing function: given map version `v` with ranges and a key, return the owner; given a reply stamped `v + 1` (your fixture's choice; Lab 5 sends a bare `ErrWrongGroup`), describe the client refresh and retry. Sketch the three movement states (serving old, migrating, serving new) and say where each request lands.
traps: Caching the map without its version. The client cannot detect staleness, so correctness rests entirely on servers rejecting keys they no longer own.
Treating a redirect as failure. `ErrWrongGroup` is the normal path during movement; fetching the config and retrying is correct.
Dropping in-flight requests at cutover. The new owner serves, but requests already sent to the old owner need forwarding or retry, never silent drops.

selfTest.q: A client holds map v5 while the shard moved in v6. What tells the client?
selfTest.a: In Lab 5 the old group replies `ErrWrongGroup`, which carries no config number. The clerk queries the controller for the latest config and retries against the new owner. Your own fixture may also stamp replies with the installed map version.

selfTest.q: Why must the map version ride on every assignment instead of shipping the shard list alone?
selfTest.a: Without versions two maps cannot be ordered. Numbers order the maps, but a stale writer is fenced only once its group has frozen the shard or learned the newer number and rejects older work.

selfTest.q: Gossip versus ZooKeeper for distributing the map: what changes?
selfTest.a: Gossip is fast but can leave two sides with different owners for one shard. ZooKeeper or etcd gives one authoritative map through consensus.

selfTest.q: A read arrives at the old owner after cutover. What is correct?
selfTest.a: Forward it to the new owner or redirect the client there. Never serve stale data as current and never drop the request.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: versioned map routing, stale-route injection, and movement tests with no double ownership.
units.stopWhen: Your map routes a seeded key set across a join, a stale client recovers through redirects, and a movement test shows single ownership throughout.

fit.note: DDIA gives routing and coordination options and Lab 5 gives the versioned-config mechanism; implementation practice lives in the section mini-project.

units.title: Replication-aware placement, online shard movement and ownership epochs
outcomes: Place three replicas of each shard in three failure domains so losing any one domain leaves a majority.
Move a shard by freeze, install and delete under numbered configs while unaffected shards keep serving.
Recover an interrupted move from stored current and next configurations.
units.why: Moving a shard while clients write to it is where data is lost or doubled. Numbered configs order the moves, and freezing the source before the destination serves keeps exactly one owner accepting writes for each key.

next.note: Measure the move: traffic, cutover pause and availability.
Compare shard movement with consumer-group rebalance.

study.title: Hot spots, splits and who runs rebalancing
study.locator: Chapter 7, Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots and Operations: Automatic Versus Manual Rebalancing (pp. 263-265): hot keys, shard splits, automatic versus manual control and the cascading-failure warning

study.title: Replicas on distinct machines and racks
study.locator: Section 12, Replication on the Ring: walk clockwise to distinct physical servers, skip virtual nodes of a machine already used, and spread replicas across racks or zones
study.depth: For a majority of three replicas to survive any one domain loss, use three independent failure domains.

study.title: Freeze, install, delete with numbered configs
study.locator: Lab 5 Sharded KV (Spring 2026), Parts A and B: ChangeConfigTo as FreezeShard, InstallShard and DeleteShard fenced by config Num, InitController recovery from stored current and next configurations, and the Part D note that cross-shard transactions need two-phase commit with two-phase locking

study.title: Ownership epochs as the movement contract
study.locator: The partition rebalance with ownership epochs stretch goal with the correctness rule that stale epochs cannot mutate current ownership

focus: Placement is two decisions: which keys form a shard and which failure domains hold its replicas. Correlated failures kill shards stacked on one rack.

Lab 5 freezes the moving shard before copying, installs it at the destination, deletes the frozen copy and publishes the new configuration. Writes to the moving shard retry during the pause while other shards keep serving; copying while still serving needs a catch-up or forwarding protocol the lab does not supply.

The config number is an ownership epoch for migration: a group that has seen a higher number rejects shard RPCs carrying older ones. Client Get and Put carry no number, so the frozen or deleted shard state is what turns them away.
Automatic rebalancing can cascade. A slow node misdiagnosed as dead triggers moves that overload the rest, so DDIA keeps a human in the loop.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, walk a move of one shard from group 1 to group 2: freeze, state copy, install at the new config number, delete. Show what a write to the moving shard gets during the copy (the frozen source rejects it and the clerk retries) and which number the destination checks on install.
traps: Deleting the old copy before the new owner serves. A crash between copy and cutover then loses the shard.
Ordering owners by wall-clock time. Epochs must be monotonic numbers from the controller, never timestamps.
Moving many shards at once for speed. Parallel moves multiply transfer traffic and stall serving; move, verify, then repeat.

selfTest.q: A shard keeps 3 replicas on one rack and the rack switch dies. What happens?
selfTest.a: The whole shard goes dark despite 3 copies. Put the three replicas in three failure domains so one correlated failure leaves a majority.

selfTest.q: A client with an old config sends a Put for a moved shard to its old owner. What stops it?
selfTest.a: The old group froze and then deleted the shard, so it answers `ErrWrongGroup`; the clerk queries the controller and retries at the new owner. Migration RPCs carrying an older config number fail the number check.

selfTest.q: Why does DDIA warn against fully automatic rebalancing?
selfTest.a: Moves are expensive and failure detection can be wrong. A slow node suspected dead triggers moves that worsen overload into cascading failure.

selfTest.q: A controller dies mid-move and a new one starts. What must it recover?
selfTest.a: The stored current and next configurations, so it completes the interrupted move instead of starting a conflicting one.

practice.name: MIT 6.5840 Lab 5 Sharded KV, Parts A and B
practice.locator: Implement the shardctrler, shardgrp server and clerk in src/shardkv1. Run Part A (`make RUN="-run 5A" shardkv`, from TestInitQuery5A through the join and leave movement tests) and Part B (controller recovery after failure)
practice.note: Optional integrated path if your MIT Labs 2 to 4 already work: complete Parts A and B and keep your solution private. Otherwise the section mini-project covers this: a local freeze, install and delete fixture with controller restart, persisted current and next configs and delayed stale-RPC tests. Part C adds concurrent controller arbitration.

units.stopWhen: You move a shard between two local groups under continuous writes, no write lands on two owners, and a killed and restarted controller resumes the move.

fit.note: DDIA covers rebalance trade-offs, AlgoMaster covers replica placement and Lab 5 covers numbered movement with recovery; its public tests are the checked practice once Labs 2 to 4 work, and the mini-project fixture otherwise.

units.title: Hot keys, load skew and scatter-gather tail latency
outcomes: Quantify per-shard load from a key distribution and price a hot-key split as write relief against read fan-out.
Derive scatter-gather latency from per-shard latency distributions, including the tail.
Measure skew and tails on your machine with fixed seeds and labeled setups.
units.why: Uniform hashing balances data, not traffic. One hot key can saturate a shard while the cluster idles, and every cross-shard query waits for the slowest shard.

next.note: Run scatter-gather against secondary indexes.
Measure skew and tails in your own harness.

study.title: Hot spots and the split-key remedy
study.locator: Chapter 7, Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots (pp. 263-264): hot shards and keys, isolating a hot key, the random-digit suffix split with its read and bookkeeping costs

study.title: Why scatter queries amplify tails
study.locator: Chapter 7, Sharding and Secondary Indexes on local indexes (p. 269): scatter to all shards with tail latency amplification and the scaling limit it sets

focus: Skew is about access, not data size. Equal key counts still overload one shard when one key takes most traffic.
Splitting a hot write key with a random suffix divides writes by the suffix count but multiplies the read fan-out by the same factor.

With concurrent dispatch, the shard-wait part of scatter-gather latency is the slowest shard's time, plus dispatch and merge. Without added contention, parallel dispatch beats serial calls at every percentile, but waiting for all shards amplifies the tail relative to one shard.
Read-hot and write-hot keys need different fixes: replicate or cache hot reads, split hot writes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute loads for keys `[10, 20, 30, 40]` over 4 shards (`[2, 0, 2, 0]`) and name the hot shards. Then take one hot key at 10,000 writes per second, split it across 100 suffix keys, and state the expected write rate per split key with the new read fan-out.
traps: Adding shards to fix a hot key. The key still hashes to one shard; only splitting or replicating the key helps.
Averaging shard latencies for scatter-gather. The query waits for the slowest shard, so report the maximum and the tail.
Splitting every key preemptively. Tracking which keys are split costs more than it saves for cold keys.

selfTest.q: Four shards hold loads `[2, 0, 2, 0]`. Is the cluster balanced?
selfTest.a: No. Shards 0 and 2 hold everything while 1 and 3 idle. The skew comes from key choice, not data size.

selfTest.q: A hot key takes 10,000 writes per second and gets a two-digit suffix split. What is the per-key rate and the read cost?
selfTest.a: About 100 writes per second per split key. Each read now fans out to 100 keys and combines the results.

selfTest.q: Ten shards each show p99 of 20 ms and a query waits for all ten. What is the scatter-gather p99?
selfTest.a: Not determined by the p99s alone. If shard times are independent with the same continuous distribution, all ten finish within 20 ms with probability \(0.99^{10} \approx 0.904\), so the scatter p99 sits near the single-shard p99.9. Perfectly correlated shards would not amplify it at all.

selfTest.q: A celebrity key is read-hot but rarely written. Split it or replicate it?
selfTest.a: Replicate or cache it. Splitting relieves writes but multiplies reads, which is exactly the wrong trade here.

practice.name: AlgoMaster Calculate Hash Shard Load, skewed case
practice.locator: Example 2 ([10, 20, 30, 40], 4) gives `[2, 0, 2, 0]`. Extend it with a 100-way hot-key split and report per-key writes with read fan-out
practice.note: This drills load arithmetic only. Tail-latency measurement runs in the skew measurement unit and the mini-project.

units.stopWhen: You quantify a skewed distribution by hand and can price a split as write relief against read fan-out and a scatter as tail from the maximum.

fit.note: DDIA derives hot-key splits and scatter tails at the unit depth; the skewed drill checks load arithmetic and the mini-project checks tails.

units.title: Local and global secondary indexes, cross-shard aggregation and CDC-maintained indexes
outcomes: Contrast local and global secondary indexes on query fan-out and write cost.
Price a secondary-index query as postings lookup, network intersection, record fetch and top-K merge.
Describe CDC-maintained index updates and their staleness window.
units.why: Sharding by primary key breaks every other access path. Each secondary query either fans out to all shards or maintains a second sharded index that writes must keep in sync.

next.note: Feed CDC-maintained indexes through the outbox relay.
Use change data capture as the maintenance feed.

study.title: Local and global secondary indexes
study.locator: Chapter 7, Sharding and Secondary Indexes (pp. 268-271): local indexes with Figure 7-9, term-partitioned global indexes with Figure 7-10, the write-sync cost and DynamoDB async staleness

study.title: Outbox relay as the index maintenance feed
study.locator: The outbox pattern: one local transaction writes the business row plus the outbox row, Debezium tails the WAL, delivery is at-least-once so consumers stay idempotent

focus: Local indexes write with the record but reads by value fan out to all shards. Global indexes answer one term from one shard but every write touches index shards.
A global index is itself sharded data: term-partitioned postings live apart from the records they point to, so fetching records re-fans out.

A top-K query fans out, takes each shard's local top K and merges them; the merge is cheap, and the fan-out and slowest shard set the cost. Distributed joins wait for the later unit on distributed dataflow graphs, shuffle and operator parallelism.

An index maintained asynchronously from CDC can lag the source. Its staleness includes capture, broker, consumer and apply delay, not just relay lag, and convergence assumes changes are retained and applied in order.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the red-cars postings for two shards under local versus global indexing: where `color:red` lives in each case, which shards a `color = red` query touches, and which shards a record fetch touches.
traps: Assuming a global index keeps reads single-shard end to end. Postings sit on one index shard, but the records they point to still live on many shards.
Hand-rolling a value-to-ID map without transactions. Races and partial writes desync it; DDIA warns about exactly this on p. 269.
Treating CDC-maintained indexes as current. Reads miss everything the index has not yet applied, and relay lag is only one part of that delay.

selfTest.q: A user table is sharded by user ID with a local email index. What does a lookup by email cost?
selfTest.a: A fan-out to all shards plus a combine, since matching rows may sit on any shard. Cheap writes, expensive secondary reads.

selfTest.q: A global color index holds `color:red` on index shard 0. Which shards serve the query and the record fetch?
selfTest.a: One index shard serves the postings. Fetching the red-car records fans out again to every shard that owns those IDs.

selfTest.q: An AND of two terms living on different index shards has long postings. What is the cost?
selfTest.a: Shipping postings over the network to intersect them. Short postings are cheap; long ones make the query slow.

selfTest.q: The index's applied position trails the source by 5 seconds. What may an index read miss?
selfTest.a: Writes from those 5 seconds. Measure lag at the index's applied position: relay lag alone leaves out broker and apply delay.

practice.name: AlgoMaster Merge Cross-Shard Top-K Results
practice.locator: Implement `topK(shardScores, k)` over per-shard descending streams with a heap. Example 1 ([[9, 7, 3], [8, 6], [10, 5]], 4) gives `[10, 9, 8, 7]`
practice.note: Drills the merge side of scatter-gather. It does not move data or measure tails.

units.stopWhen: You place postings for both index kinds without notes and can price a cross-shard query as fan-out plus merge.

fit.note: DDIA covers local and global indexes with postings costs at explain depth and the HLD outbox section covers CDC maintenance; the merge drill checks top-K aggregation.

units.title: ACID boundaries, dirty and nonrepeatable reads, lost updates and write skew
outcomes: Draw the ACID boundary and say which letter each failure threatens.
Construct dirty-write, lost-update, read-skew and write-skew histories.
Classify anomalies with the Berenson P0 to P4, A5A and A5B names and say which ones snapshot isolation still admits.
units.why: Isolation levels are names for which anomalies they admit. Without the anomaly shapes the names are marketing; with them each level is a testable claim. The Systems unit on transactions and isolation anomalies built the doctor write-skew history under PostgreSQL. Here the new work is Berenson's phenomenon names and what Maelstrom's weak-model checkers can and cannot detect.

next.note: Prevent the anomalies with locking.
Prevent them with snapshots instead.

study.title: What a transaction promises
study.locator: Chapter 8, What Exactly Is a Transaction (pp. 278-288): The Meaning of ACID, Single-Object and Multi-Object Operations, Figure 8-1 and the retry caveats just before Weak Isolation Levels

study.title: Weak isolation and the doctor on-call skew
study.locator: Chapter 8, Weak Isolation Levels (pp. 288-307): Read Committed with dirty reads and writes, Snapshot Isolation with read skew in Figure 8-6, Preventing Lost Updates, and Write Skew and Phantoms with the on-call example in Figure 8-8

study.title: Phenomena P0 to P3 with snapshot anomalies
study.locator: Sections 2 and 3 with Tables 1 to 3 for P0 to P3; Section 4.1 for P4 lost update; Section 4.2 for snapshot isolation, A5A read skew and A5B write skew; Table 4 for which levels admit each
study.depth: Cite these definitions, not the SQL-92 prose they correct.

study.title: The transfer that must not half-happen
study.locator: The bank-transfer motivation and the ACID definitions: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability

focus: ACID consistency means your invariants hold; it says nothing about replicas or timing. Isolation is the concurrency half, atomicity plus durability the failure half.
Dirty reads see uncommitted data, nonrepeatable reads see committed change between two reads, lost updates merge two writes into one, write skew merges two reads into a broken invariant.
Write skew generalizes lost update: different transactions updating different objects after reading the same set.

Retry the whole transaction after a definite abort; a rolled-back transaction left nothing to duplicate. A commit whose acknowledgement timed out has an unknown outcome: check its status or retry with a stable ID and atomic deduplication.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write four short histories on two transactions and name each with Berenson's terms: a dirty write (P0), a lost update (P4), read skew (A5A) and write skew (A5B). For each, say whether snapshot isolation forbids it, then check your answers against Table 4.
traps: Calling snapshot isolation serializable. Oracle sells a level named serializable that is snapshot isolation; it admits write skew.
Blaming the database for a retry double-apply. A commit that timed out before its ack reruns unless the application dedups.
Treating phantoms as exotic. Any check-then-insert over usernames or bookings is a phantom risk under snapshot isolation.

selfTest.q: One transaction writes x = 3 without committing and another reads x. Which anomaly, and which level admits it?
selfTest.a: Dirty read (P1). Only read-uncommitted admits it; PostgreSQL has no such mode and behaves as read-committed instead.

selfTest.q: Aaliyah and Bryce both read 2 on call, both go off call, both commit. Name it and say why snapshot isolation allows it.
selfTest.a: A5B write skew. Each transaction updated a different object, so no write-write conflict fired and both snapshots looked safe.

selfTest.q: Two clients read-modify-write one counter and the total rises by 1, not 2. Which anomaly and cheapest fix?
selfTest.a: Lost update. Use an atomic increment such as `UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1` or a compare-and-set retry loop.

selfTest.q: A booking app checks for overlaps then inserts, twice concurrently. What breaks?
selfTest.a: A phantom: both checks pass on empty results, then both inserts land overlapping. Snapshot isolation needs serializable isolation or materialized conflict locks here.

practice.name: Gossip Glomers 6a: single-node transactions
practice.locator: Serve the `txn-rw-register` workload on one node: `./maelstrom test -w txn-rw-register --bin ~/go/bin/maelstrom-txn --node-count 1 --time-limit 20 --rate 1000 --concurrency 2n --consistency-models read-uncommitted --availability total`

practice.locator: Replicate writes to both nodes and run the base plus the partition case (`--availability total --nemesis partition`). G0 (dirty write) is the only prohibited anomaly
practice.note: The page states its checker cannot detect G0 anomalies, so a pass here is weaker than its label.

practice.name: Gossip Glomers 6c: read-committed under partition

units.stopWhen: You write the four histories from memory, classify each with its Berenson name and say which one snapshot isolation admits.

fit.note: DDIA plus Berenson define every anomaly at explain depth; Maelstrom 6a to 6c give checked weak-model practice.

units.title: Serializability, strict serializability, two-phase locking and deadlocks
outcomes: Test a history for serializability by finding an equivalent serial order.
Implement two-phase locking with shared, exclusive and predicate locks.
Detect a deadlock cycle and resolve it by abort with client retry.
units.why: Serializability is the contract every weaker level approximates. Two-phase locking buys it with waiting, and deadlocks are the price. The Systems unit on two-phase locking, timestamp ordering and MVCC taught the mechanisms and conflict graphs. Here the new work is a lock manager with predicate protection and deadlock detection, and the real-time order that strict serializability adds.

next.note: Trade blocking for aborts with snapshots.
Add atomic commit across shards to isolated execution.

study.title: Serial execution, 2PL and predicate locks
study.locator: Chapter 8, Serializability (pp. 308-317): Actual Serial Execution, Two-Phase Locking with shared and exclusive modes and deadlocks, predicate locks for phantoms and materializing conflicts as a last resort

study.title: Serializable orders with strong strict 2PL
study.locator: Lecture 11 (Spring 2026), concurrency-control half: the bank-transfer serializable orders, strong strict two-phase locking rules, the T3/T4 deadlock with timeout and wound-wait resolution

study.title: Row locks and the deadlock example
study.locator: Section 13.3, especially 13.3.2 row-level locks (`FOR UPDATE` and `FOR SHARE`) and 13.3.4 Deadlocks with the two-accounts update cycle

study.title: Serializability versus strict serializability
study.locator: Chapter 10, the box Linearizability Versus Serializability (pp. 407-408): serializability allows stale reads, linearizability adds recency, and the combination is strict serializability

focus: Serializable means some serial order explains all outputs and effects; test it by enumerating orders, as the lecture does. Strict serializability adds real time: a transaction that starts after another commits must follow it in that order.
Strong strict 2PL acquires before use and holds past commit. Releasing early reopens the interleavings that locks were meant to close.
Read-write sharing needs two modes: shared for readers, exclusive for writers. Phantoms need predicate locks, not row locks.
Deadlock needs a cycle. Prevention orders lock acquisition; detection aborts a participant. Either way the client retries.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run the lecture bank example with `x = 10` and `y = 10`: `T1` transfers 1 while `T2` audits. List the two serializable outcomes and show two interleavings that are not serializable. Then show the `T3`/`T4` deadlock on `get(x)` and `get(y)` and resolve it by aborting one. Finally give a two-transaction history that is serializable but not strictly serializable.
traps: Holding locks to end of statement instead of end of transaction. Early release breaks serializability even with correct acquisition.
Locking rows to stop phantoms. No rows exist yet to lock; the fix is a predicate lock or materialized conflict rows.
Retrying a deadlock abort in the same order at once. The same cycle can reform; order locks consistently or back off before retry.

selfTest.q: What are the serializable outcomes of the lecture bank example?
selfTest.a: `T1` then `T2` prints 11 and 9; `T2` then `T1` prints 10 and 10. Any other printed pair is not serializable.

selfTest.q: `T2` releases `x` after its first read and `T1` runs between the two reads. Result and verdict?
selfTest.a: `T2` prints 10 and 9, which matches neither serial order. Holding the lock to commit would have blocked `T1`.

selfTest.q: Two bookings check-then-insert concurrently. Why do row locks not help?
selfTest.a: The conflicting rows do not exist yet, so there is nothing to lock. The fix is a predicate lock on the search condition or serializable isolation.

selfTest.q: PostgreSQL detects a deadlock. Which transaction aborts?
selfTest.a: Unpredictable by design. The application must retry any transaction that fails with a deadlock, not a chosen one.

practice.name: AlgoMaster Analyze Transaction Serializability
practice.locator: Implement `isSerializable` and `serialOrder` through the conflict graph. The `W(x)` then `R(x)` case is serializable with order [1, 2]; the `x: 1 to 2` plus `y: 2 to 1` case is not
practice.note: Drills conflict-serializability only. The section mini-project covers this: a shared and exclusive lock manager with growing and shrinking phases, predicate or range protection, wait-for-cycle detection with abort, and a real-time-order history test.

units.stopWhen: You classify the bank interleavings, build a conflict graph for a new schedule and give a serializable history that strict serializability rejects, all without notes.

fit.note: DDIA, the MIT lecture and the PostgreSQL locking reference reach derive and implement depth; the drill checks conflict graphs.

units.title: Timestamp ordering, optimistic concurrency, MVCC and read-only snapshot coordination
outcomes: Contrast timestamp ordering and optimistic validation with pessimistic locking.
Decide tuple visibility from snapshots and version chains, and state what the collector may free.
Serve read-only snapshots across shards at one agreed timestamp, waiting on each shard until its safe time reaches it.
units.why: Blocking every reader behind writers stalls read-heavy workloads. Snapshots let reads run lock-free on a consistent past, and optimistic checks move the cost of conflict to commit time.

next.note: Commit snapshot-isolated work atomically across shards.
Compare snapshot reads with session guarantees.

study.title: Timestamp ordering and multiversioning lectures
study.locator: Fall 2025 Lectures #19 (Timestamp Ordering Concurrency Control) and #20 (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): basic timestamp ordering, optimistic concurrency and MVCC version storage

study.title: Snapshots, visibility and lost-update prevention
study.locator: Chapter 5, Sections 5.5 to 5.8 (page read 2026-10-15): transaction snapshots, visibility check rules, hint bits and phantoms in repeatable read, and first-updater-wins; Section 5.9 for the SSI dangerous structure
study.depth: Lock modes live in the PostgreSQL locking reference from the previous unit, not here.

study.title: MVCC chains with optimistic control
study.locator: Chapter 8 (pp. 295-299): multiversion chains with `inserted_by` and `deleted_by`, visibility and garbage collection; plus Pessimistic versus optimistic concurrency control (pp. 318-319)

study.title: Lock-free reads at a safe timestamp
study.locator: Sections 4.1.3 (Serving Reads at Timestamp) and 4.2.2 (Read-Only Transactions): the safe-time rule, and read-only transactions that pick one timestamp, may wait for safe time to advance, and take no locks

focus: Timestamp ordering stamps operations and rejects late arrivals; optimistic control runs free and validates at commit. In their basic forms, both abort instead of waiting.
MVCC keeps old versions tagged with writer IDs and a snapshot decides visibility. The collector frees only versions invisible to every active snapshot.

PostgreSQL repeatable read is snapshot isolation: plain reads never wait for row write locks. A second updater of the same row waits for the first; if the first commits, the second fails with a serialization error and retries the whole transaction.
A distributed read-only snapshot needs one timestamp valid on all shards. Each shard reading its own latest is not a consistent snapshot.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw two row versions of an account (500 marked deleted by transaction 13, 400 inserted by 13) and decide visibility for a snapshot that started before 13 committed. State when the collector may remove the 500 version.
traps: Freeing a version that one snapshot still sees. Long-running snapshots pin old versions; the collector cannot free what any snapshot reads.
Assuming snapshot isolation is serializable. The doctor example commits under snapshots; only SSI checks or locks stop it.
Reading each shard at its own latest timestamp and calling it consistent. Cross-shard reads need one agreed timestamp.

selfTest.q: How is an update stored under MVCC?
selfTest.a: As a delete plus an insert: the old version is marked with the deleter ID and a new version is inserted. Both stay until no snapshot can see the old one.

selfTest.q: Two snapshot transactions update the same row. What happens?
selfTest.a: In PostgreSQL repeatable read the second updater waits for the first. If the first commits, the second fails with a concurrent-update serialization error and retries the whole transaction; if the first aborts, the second proceeds.

selfTest.q: An analytics snapshot stays open for hours. What is the storage effect?
selfTest.a: It pins every version it can see. The table bloats until the snapshot closes and vacuum frees the dead versions.

selfTest.q: How does Spanner serve a read-only transaction without locks?
selfTest.a: It picks one read timestamp for the whole transaction. Each replica serves once its safe time reaches that timestamp, which accounts for applied Paxos writes and unresolved prepared transactions, so reads take no locks but may wait. The result is externally consistent, not stale by design.

practice.name: CMU 15-445 Homework 5, Questions 3 and 4
practice.locator: Question 3 (optimistic concurrency control) and Question 4 (multi-version concurrency control)
practice.note: Project 4 (https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2025/project4/) is optional C++ practice if your earlier BusTub projects already work. The section mini-project covers this: two shards with version selection and reclamation, and one shared read timestamp that waits for each shard's safe time.

units.stopWhen: You decide visibility for a version chain from a snapshot and can say which anomalies your snapshot still admits.

fit.note: CMU lectures plus the PostgreSQL internals chapters reach implement depth on ordering, MVCC and snapshots; Spanner covers the distributed read-only case.

units.title: Two-phase commit states, durable prepare, coordinator failure and in-doubt recovery
outcomes: Walk coordinator and participant states through prepare, commit, abort and every crash window.
Implement durable prepare and coordinator decision logging with in-doubt recovery.
Explain why a prepared participant blocks and when manual or heuristic resolution applies.
units.why: Atomic commit across shards is the one place where a crash leaves the database unsure of the outcome. The protocol earns its keep not on the happy path but in the exact recovery for each window.

next.note: Choose saga compensation where blocking is unacceptable.
Model-check the protocol you just implemented.

study.title: The coordinator and participant exchange
study.locator: Chapter 8, Two-Phase Commit (pp. 324-328): partial multi-node commit in Figure 8-12, the successful exchange in Figure 8-13, durable prepare and the coordinator decision record on p. 326, and coordinator failure with an in-doubt participant in Figure 8-14

study.title: Blocking, heuristics and XA limits
study.locator: Chapter 8 (pp. 328-333): coordinator failure with locks held, three-phase commit limits, heuristic decisions as a catastrophic escape hatch, and single-coordinator failure modes
study.depth: Read three-phase commit as a caution, not an assignment. This section leaves 3PC for later.

study.title: TIDs, tentative writes and forget rules
study.locator: Lecture 11 (Spring 2026), distributed half: transaction IDs on every message, tentative writes, participant disk write before YES, coordinator COMMIT log write, blocking after YES, forget-after-ACK rules, and Raft versus 2PC

focus: Prepare is a promise backed by disk. A YES voter must keep enough state across a reboot to obey either COMMIT or ABORT from the coordinator, so tentative writes and lock ownership persist before the vote.
The commit point is one coordinator disk write. Before it the coordinator may abort, and a recovering coordinator treats an unlogged transaction as aborted; after it, recovery resends COMMIT.
A YES voter that hears nothing blocks. Commit and abort are both still possible, so guessing either way breaks atomicity.
2PC gives atomicity, not availability: every participant must be up. Replicating each role is what adds availability.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, walk the crash matrix: participant down before durable prepare (it may abort), after durable prepare but before YES is sent (it recovers in doubt and asks), after YES (the same), coordinator down before the commit record (recovery aborts) and after it (recovery resends COMMIT). Show why a prepared participant cannot time out and abort, using one side committed with the other unknown.
traps: Committing on unilateral timeout after voting YES. The coordinator may have committed elsewhere; timeout-abort splits the outcome.
Reapplying a duplicate COMMIT without transaction-ID dedup. A recovered participant that forgot must ACK duplicates, not reapply them.
Calling 2PC highly available because it survives some crashes. It blocks on coordinator loss with locks held; availability needs replicated roles.

selfTest.q: A participant votes YES, then crashes before COMMIT arrives. What happens on recovery?
selfTest.a: It replays prepared state from disk, keeps holding its locks, and asks the coordinator. It commits or aborts on the coordinator answer.

selfTest.q: The coordinator crashes after logging COMMIT but before sending it out. How does recovery preserve atomicity?
selfTest.a: It reads its log, finds the COMMIT record, and resends COMMIT to every participant. The decision was already made, so resending is safe.

selfTest.q: The coordinator log disk is lost entirely. Is there an automatic recovery?
selfTest.a: No. An administrator must resolve each in-doubt transaction by inspecting participants and applying one outcome everywhere.

selfTest.q: A participant unilaterally commits an in-doubt transaction during a coordinator outage. Verdict?
selfTest.a: It breaks the promise system and risks split outcomes. Heuristic decisions are a catastrophic escape hatch, never routine.

practice.name: DSLabs Lab 4 Part 3: transactions over sharded groups
practice.locator: Implement the transactional store with two-phase commit and read/write locking over Paxos groups. Run `run-tests.py --lab 4 --part 3` and read any failing trace before changing code
practice.note: Optional Java 21 path after the earlier DSLabs labs; it assumes a live majority per group and does not test disk-backed restart. The section mini-project covers this: durable prepare and decision records, a restart at each persistence boundary, and duplicate decisions.

practice.name: Building Distributed Systems: two-phase commit and coordinator failure (TW-1, TW-2)
practice.locator: TW-1 PREPARE, vote, COMMIT and ABORT exchange plus TW-2 coordinator logging with recovery from the log
practice.note: Free browser-graded drills; they do not replace the DSLabs fault tests. TW-3 stays out: three-phase commit is later work.

units.stopWhen: You walk every crash window without notes and your fixture recovers correctly from a restart at each persistence boundary.

fit.note: DDIA plus the MIT lecture derive every state and window; the mini-project fixture tests durable recovery, and DSLabs Part 3 and the drills give optional protocol practice.

units.title: Saga orchestration and choreography and compensation semantics
outcomes: Define a saga as sequenced local transactions with application-defined compensations.
Contrast orchestration with choreography on visibility and failure handling.
Name irreversible steps and place them where failure cannot strand them.
units.why: Cross-service work cannot hold database locks while waiting on other services. Sagas trade atomicity for progress, and the compensations are where the business logic really lives.

next.note: Deliver saga steps through an outbox.
Run the saga on a durable workflow with reconciliation.

study.title: Sagas with compensating transactions
study.locator: The whole paper: a saga as a sequence of transactions with compensating transactions run in reverse to amend partial execution, forward and backward recovery, and designing around steps that cannot be compensated

study.title: Orchestrated versus choreographed sagas
study.locator: Sagas: orchestrated versus choreographed coordination, the missing isolation guarantee, and when not to use distributed transactions

study.title: Why 2PC fails the checkout
study.locator: The e-commerce order example: order, inventory, payment and shipping services, why prepare-and-wait locking fails across them, and what the saga coordinates instead

focus: A saga is not a transaction: steps commit independently, so other work sees partial progress. Compensation amends; it never rolls back.
Orchestration puts the sequence in one controller, which is visible and has one place to fix. Choreography puts it in event reactions, which decouples services but scatters the trace.
Compensations are application code with their own failures. A non-idempotent or failing compensation leaves the saga half-undone.

Some effects cannot be physically undone: an email cannot be unsent, though a correction can compensate it in business terms. Put genuinely noncompensatable effects after the fallible compensatable work, define forward recovery past that pivot, and keep unknown outcomes for reconciliation.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write an order saga (reserve, charge, ship, notify) with each step compensation, fail at ship, and list the compensation order. State which step is irreversible and where you placed it.
traps: Compensating in forward order. Undo runs in reverse: the last completed step is compensated first.
Assuming saga steps are isolated. Concurrent sagas interleave and partial progress is visible; business rules must tolerate it.
Retrying a failed step forever. Some failures need compensation, not retry; decide per step which path applies.

selfTest.q: A four-step saga fails at step 3. Which compensations run, in what order?
selfTest.a: If step 3 definitely failed without a committed effect, compensate step 2 first, then step 1; step 4 never started. If step 3's outcome is unknown, query or replay its stable identity before choosing the recovery path.

selfTest.q: Where does failure debugging happen under orchestration versus choreography?
selfTest.a: The saga coordinator logs the sequence centrally. Choreography spreads it across service event logs that must be correlated.

selfTest.q: Payment is captured, shipment fails, and the refund API is down. What is the saga state?
selfTest.a: Stuck mid-compensation. The refund needs retry with ownership, plus reconciliation; silent abort would hide taken money.

selfTest.q: Why can two-phase commit not cover the external payment provider?
selfTest.a: The provider exposes no prepare-and-wait interface, so it cannot promise to commit later. No global atomic commit is possible.

practice.name: AlgoMaster Build a Saga Compensation Order
practice.locator: Implement `compensationOrder(steps, failAt)` returning completed steps in reverse. Example 1 ([reserve, charge, ship, notify], 2) gives [charge, reserve]; failing at 0 gives empty
practice.note: Drills compensation ordering only. Failure detection, retries and irreversible steps run in the durable-workflow unit and the mini-project.

units.stopWhen: You write a four-step saga with compensations from memory and can argue orchestration versus choreography for it.

fit.note: The Sagas paper defines compensation semantics and the HLD plus AlgoMaster lessons contrast coordination styles; the drill checks ordering.

units.title: Transactional outbox and inbox, idempotent steps and the exactly-once effect boundary
outcomes: Implement the transactional outbox with a relay that is at-least-once by design.
Make steps idempotent with keys and dedup state, ordered per aggregate by sequence.
Draw the exactly-once effect boundary for a new workflow.
units.why: Dual writes to a database plus a broker fail independently. The outbox turns two systems into one local transaction plus an at-least-once relay, and idempotency turns redelivery into safety.

next.note: Run outbox-fed steps under reconciliation.
Carry the effect boundary into delivery semantics.

study.title: The idempotent receiver without distributed transactions
study.locator: Chapter 8, Exactly-Once Message Processing Revisited (pp. 334-335): the processed message-ID table, the four-step receiver with its separate cleanup transaction, and the sharded extension

study.title: Outbox with CDC relay
study.locator: The outbox pattern: the dual-write problem, one local transaction for business row plus outbox row, Debezium WAL tailing, at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers

study.title: Keys, dedup stores and TTL sizing
study.locator: Idempotency fundamentals, the idempotency-key pattern with request fingerprint and replayed responses, and consumer-side dedup (`SET NX`, `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) with TTL sized past the retry window
study.depth: Skip the standalone Redis marker recipe: setting the marker before a separate processing step can lose an effect after a crash, and the printed argument order is invalid (the form is `SET key value NX EX seconds`). The dedup row and the effect belong in one transaction, as in DDIA.

study.title: Dual writes with safe retries
study.locator: The dual-write problem and the outbox relay with delivery, ordering, retry and cleanup notes, read with the idempotency lesson on safe retries

focus: The outbox row commits with the business row or neither commits. The relay may lag or duplicate but never invents events.

Idempotency keys turn retries into no-ops only when the key insert, the effect and the stored result commit in one transaction; a concurrent duplicate then fails on the unique key. Replay the stored result after commit, and rely on the endpoint's own deduplication for external effects.
Per-aggregate sequences enforce order: apply only the next sequence, reject duplicates, and park gaps for redelivery.
Exactly-once covers effects inside the boundary (database plus acknowledged processing). External sends such as email can still duplicate.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement the ordered consumer for `acct-1`: `apply("acct-1", 1, 100)` twice, then `apply("acct-1", 3, 25)` and `apply("acct-1", 2, 50)`. Expect `APPLIED`, `DUPLICATE`, `GAP` and `APPLIED`, with balance 150 and last sequence 2. Redeliver sequence 3 with increment 25 and expect balance 175 and last sequence 3.
traps: Publishing before committing. A crash between publish and commit emits events for rolled-back work; write the outbox row inside the transaction.

Deleting the current message ID before the broker acknowledgement is durable. In DDIA's four-step receiver the ID goes in a separate transaction after the acknowledgement; a source that can replay keeps dedup state for its whole replay horizon.
Calling at-least-once delivery exactly-once processing. Delivery duplicates; only the idempotent boundary makes effects once.

selfTest.q: An order service writes the order, then publishes, and crashes between the two. What breaks without an outbox?
selfTest.a: The order exists but no event ships, so downstream services never reserve or bill. The outbox writes row and event atomically instead.

selfTest.q: The relay delivers one event twice. What does the consumer do?
selfTest.a: The second apply sees a sequence at or below the last applied one, returns `DUPLICATE`, and changes nothing.

selfTest.q: Sequence 5 arrives while the last applied is 3. What is the correct action?
selfTest.a: Return `GAP` and change nothing. Sequence 4 may still arrive by redelivery; applying 5 now would skip it.

selfTest.q: A retry resends an email step inside the boundary. What is guaranteed?
selfTest.a: Nothing. External sends escape the boundary. Send after commit with its own dedup key or accept possible duplicates.

practice.name: AlgoMaster Consume Outbox Events Idempotently and in Order
practice.locator: Implement `apply`, `balance` and `lastSequence` with `DUPLICATE`, `GAP` and `APPLIED`. The acct-1 sequences from Reproduce are the acceptance cases
practice.note: Drills consumer logic only. The relay and the processed-ID table run in the mini-project.

units.stopWhen: Your consumer passes the duplicate, gap and reorder cases and you can draw the boundary around a new workflow.

fit.note: DDIA plus the HLD outbox and idempotency chapters reach implement depth on the relay and the boundary; the drill checks consumer logic.

units.title: A durable workflow with fault tests and invariant reconciliation
outcomes: Implement a durable workflow with persisted intent, replayable steps and a reconciler.
Recover from coordinator death, ambiguous replies, duplicate steps and failed compensation.
Check terminal business conditions independently of workflow status, and distinguish pending repair from completion.
units.why: This builds on the earlier units on saga orchestration and compensation and on the transactional outbox and idempotent steps. Now durable decisions, service-side deduplication and reconciliation must work together when the coordinator dies between an effect and its reply.

next.note: Measure the workflow: latency, aborts, duplicates and recovery time.
Compare workflow checkpoints with stream checkpoints.

study.title: Sagas (SIGMOD 1987): recovery state and the recovery daemon
study.locator: Backward Recovery and Forward Recovery, printed pp. 253-254; Other Errors, pp. 254-255; Section 7, Implementing Sagas on Top of an Existing DBMS, pp. 255-256
study.depth: Focus on logged progress, save-points, failed compensation and the daemon's periodic scan. The paper assumes local database transactions; remote effects need the preceding unit's atomic deduplication boundary. Skip parallel sagas.

study.title: Ledger reconciliation and failed compensation
study.locator: When you do not need distributed transactions: linked ledger entries and reconciliation; Common Pitfalls: Compensations that do not semantically undo and Forgetting idempotency in saga compensations
study.depth: Use only these paragraphs as design review. Reconciliation does not make separate commits atomic, and a timed-out action can still complete later. Do not use the checkout solution's unresolved-payment timeout as permission to close a workflow.

study.title: Recovery evidence in loglab
study.locator: Architecture constraints; Milestone D - Failure handling; Correctness requirements; Failure-injection requirements
study.depth: Apply the durable-history, timeout-after-commit and stale-epoch requirements to the DS-6 workflow slice. Stream checkpoints and the full project's fault campaign come later.

focus: Persist step intent and stable operation identity before dispatch. Record replies durably; if a reply is missing, query or replay the same identity against an endpoint that commits deduplication and effect atomically.

Recovery must fence a replaced coordinator and respect the recorded forward or compensating decision. Compensation itself can time out, fail or repeat; retain unresolved work with bounded retries and an escalation owner.

State safety conditions that hold during pending work separately from terminal conditions. A charge awaiting refund is unresolved, not a completed cancellation; eventual repair assumes the dependency recovers or a manual path succeeds.

Reconcile service ledgers by business identity, not just workflow status. In local fault tests, pause actors before the independent scan; with live services, validate versions before an idempotent repair so a stale scan cannot reverse newer work.
units.reproduce: In Python 3 on your machine, implement a local durable order fixture with one item available and price 100 integer currency units. Each service atomically stores its effect and stable operation ID; use separate stores from coordinator state. Reserve the item, charge once, then discard the reply and restart the coordinator from persisted intent. Replaying the charge must leave total charged at 100. Make shipping definitively reject without an effect; persist the compensating decision. Fail the first refund without an effect, then restart and retry with the same refund ID. After refund and release succeed, pause actors and independently read ledgers: charged 100, refunded 100, shipped 0, available 1, reserved 0. Repeat compensation and confirm those values stay unchanged. Before the refund succeeds, the order must remain unresolved, not canceled.
traps: Treating durable intent as proof that a remote effect happened, or a missing reply as proof that it did not. Only the endpoint's durable result resolves that ambiguity.
Treating compensation as an alternative to retry safety. Even a compensatable charge must not be duplicated by an ambiguous retry.
Checking only global totals. One order's missing refund can cancel another order's duplicate refund; reconcile by order and operation identity.

selfTest.q: A charge committed but its reply and coordinator completion record were lost. What should recovery do?
selfTest.a: Recover intent, fence the prior coordinator, then query or retry the original charge identity. Atomically persisted endpoint deduplication returns the prior result without another charge. A new identity would be unsafe.

selfTest.q: The refund dependency stays unavailable. Has the cancellation passed its terminal condition?
selfTest.a: No. Keep compensation pending with bounded retry and escalation. Safety still forbids duplicate charges or refunds, but eventual cancellation needs recovery of the dependency or an explicit manual resolution.

selfTest.q: Does a charge with no shipment always prove corruption?
selfTest.a: No. It may be valid pending work. Check the workflow decision and age, and resolve unknown shipping outcomes before retrying or refunding. A terminal canceled order with an unreconciled net charge violates this fixture's contract.

selfTest.q: Why can an independent scan report a false mismatch while services are changing?
selfTest.a: Separate reads may observe different stages of progress. Pause actors for the test oracle, or use a versioned observation and revalidate before repair. A correct global total alone also misses per-order drift.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: durable intent, outbox-fed steps, coordinator-death and duplicate injection, failed compensation and invariant reconciliation.
units.stopWhen: Your retained crash trace shows a single charge, an unresolved failed refund and an idempotent completed compensation. An independent per-order check passes after recovery, and an order incorrectly marked canceled without its refund makes it fail.

fit.note: Sagas supplies persisted recovery and a scanning daemon; the pool's HLD ledger paragraphs supply reconciliation review, and loglab supplies independent fault-test practice within six hours.

units.title: Skew, movement, abort and recovery measurement
outcomes: Measure per-shard load, movement traffic and time, abort and compensation rates, duplicates and recovery time.
Compare partition or workflow policies under matched workloads and fault schedules, with raw histories behind every table.
Separate exact fixture counts, simulated time and local timing results, including runs that fail to recover.
units.why: A balanced key count can hide an overloaded shard, and a low abort rate can hide a broken isolation boundary. Measure costs together with invariant verdicts so an apparent improvement cannot come from silently dropping work.

next.note: Carry the measurement discipline into stream lag and recovery.
Label raw histories, evidence and reproduction bounds.

study.title: What to measure with which setup
study.locator: Milestone B - Instrumentation; Milestone E - Measurement / optimization; Measurement requirements; Reproducibility and Engineering judgment in the rubric
study.depth: Apply the instrumentation and open-loop load guidance to partition movement and workflow recovery. Do not build the later stream-processing measurements yet.

study.title: Reported figures are not targets
study.locator: Virtual nodes: Practical numbers and Heterogeneous capacity; Bounded-load variant, opening hot-key paragraph; Real-World Example, Vimeo's bounded-load consistent hashing in HAProxy
study.depth: Use these as hypotheses to test, not targets. Vnode counts and reported deviations do not guarantee request balance; the Vimeo figures describe its cache workload, not your database. Stop before Trade-offs.

focus: Separate logical requests, attempts, aborts and successful unique effects. Give each rate a denominator; suppressed duplicate deliveries are not duplicate committed effects. Report invariant violations alongside throughput.

Measure per-shard keys, bytes and requests separately. Count keys whose owner changes separately from bytes actually copied, including replica transfers, catch-up and retries; timestamp the cutover and record availability and tail latency during movement.

For recovery, name the start event and the completion predicate. Fault healing, coordinator restart and invariant reconciliation are different clocks; a run still pending at the observation limit has no measured completion time.

On your machine, compare a baseline and changed policy using the same workload and fault trace, then repeat across seeds. Record versions, offered load, concurrency, key sizes, durability settings, warmup, observation window, run count and spread; a seed alone cannot control OS scheduling.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a Python 3 metric extractor for this fixed synthetic fixture, not a benchmark: requests are `[0]*8 + [1]*2`, routed by `key % 2`; keys 0 through 7 change owners from `key % 3` to `key % 4`; a separate transaction history contains 12 completed attempts, three aborted and nine committed. Assert shard request counts `[8, 2]`, maximum-to-mean request load 1.6, five changed owners and attempt abort fraction 0.25. If faults heal at simulated tick 20 and the first quiescent reconciled terminal state is tick 27, recovery is seven simulated ticks, not seven seconds. Then use the extractor on retained baseline and fault-run histories from loglab; label real durations as local measurements and preserve unresolved runs.
traps: Reporting only latency of successful requests. Include errors, timeouts, pending work and achieved goodput at the stated offered load; otherwise overload can look faster.
Treating observed key movement as a universal exact fraction. It depends on the key set, hash, placement and membership change; equal key counts need not mean equal bytes or request rates.
Reporting zero aborts as a win without checking isolation, or excluding stuck recoveries from the summary. Both can reward a weaker or broken implementation.

selfTest.q: Does the fixture's five-of-eight movement result predict bytes copied?
selfTest.a: No. It counts owner changes for those keys and those modulo mappings. Byte cost also depends on record sizes, replica placement, catch-up and retransmission.

selfTest.q: Three aborts in 12 completed attempts give what abort fraction, and do they prove three failed workflows?
selfTest.a: The attempt abort fraction is 0.25. They need not be three different workflows, and a retry may eventually commit. Report logical workflow outcomes separately.

selfTest.q: Can the maximum alone decide whether a latency SLO passed?
selfTest.a: Only if the SLO is a maximum-latency bound. A percentile SLO needs that percentile over its defined request population and window, with errors and timeouts accounted for.

selfTest.q: Faults heal, but reconciliation has not finished when observation ends. What recovery time should you report?
selfTest.a: Report recovery as incomplete at the observation limit, with elapsed time and pending state. Do not invent a completion time or omit the run. Simulated ticks remain separate from measured seconds.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: matched baseline and fault runs for skew, movement, aborts, compensation, duplicate suppression and recovery, with raw histories and invariant verdicts.
units.stopWhen: The extractor passes the fixed fixture, and a matched baseline/fault table reports skew, moved keys and bytes, abort and compensation denominators, duplicate effects, latency distributions, availability and completed or pending recovery. Keep three repetitions per setup and explain one cost or negative result without weakening the invariant.

fit.note: The pool's capstone instrumentation and measurement rubric plus HLD's workload examples support the measurement job; the fixed fixture checks accounting and the mini-project supplies repeated local runs.
